questions.q: Scott's team has a rule: coverage must stay at 90%. To hit the target easily, new member Jordan writes 50 tests on entity getters and setters. What happened?
questions.hint: Did the tests go where the bugs are?

options.text: Coverage went up, but the risky spots are no safer
options.why: Getters and setters have nothing to break. The coverage number grew, but price, payment and migration code are protected no better than before.

options.text: The system got safer, because more code is tested
options.why: More tests don't make a system safer. Checking the risky spots does.

options.text: Coverage went down, because more code was added
options.why: Adding tests for getters and setters raises coverage, if anything.

options.text: The tests got faster
options.why: More tests take slightly more time, and speed is not the point or the gain here anyway.

questions.q: Where does adding extra tests pay off the most?
questions.hint: Where is the damage biggest, and where are mistakes most likely?

options.text: Discount and tax calculation
options.why: Money is directly involved, thresholds and percentages are tricky, and mistakes easily slip past a reviewer.

options.text: The handler for the outside payment webhook
options.why: It sits at the seam with an outside system, the damage is big (money), and mistakes are likely.

options.text: Simple entity getters and setters
options.why: There is nothing to break, so tests here waste time.

options.text: A tiny helper that only writes logs
options.why: Both the damage and the complexity are low. It comes after the risky spots.

questions.q: What exactly is wrong with the test below?
questions.hint: Would this test fail if the price were wrong?

options.text: It only checks that save was called, so it passes even with a wrong total
options.why: It never verifies an outcome. A refactor of the internals can break it, yet it doesn't catch the real bug.

options.text: DiscountCalculator should have been mocked too
options.why: That would hollow the test out even more. Keeping the real calculator is better.

options.text: Using $this->once() in tests is forbidden
options.why: It isn't forbidden. The problem is that this is all the test checks, and not the result.

options.text: There is nothing wrong with it
options.why: There is: the test misses bugs, and it is needlessly brittle too.

questions.q: Which of these does KernelTestCase verify best?
questions.hint: Where do you need a real container and a real database?

options.text: That a Doctrine repository query returns the right rows
options.why: Query mistakes only show up against a real database. A mock in a unit test wouldn't verify this.

options.text: The output of a date-formatting helper
options.why: It is a pure function and needs no container. A plain unit test is enough, and faster.

options.text: A full journey in the browser, from login to placing an order
options.why: That is a job for E2E (Panther or Playwright).

options.text: 10 cases for the price percentage thresholds
options.why: That is a job for a unit test and a DataProvider, which runs in milliseconds.

questions.q: The rule is "10% off from 10,000 cents ($100)". The code wrongly uses `>` instead of `>=`. Which test values catch it?
questions.hint: Which values would give the same answer with `>` and with `>=`?

options.why: Both versions give the same answer for each of these, so the bug stays hidden.
Both are above the threshold, so `>` and `>=` agree on them.
At exactly 10,000 the correct code gives 1,000 off and the buggy code gives 0, so the test fails.

options.text: Ten random amounts
options.why: The chance of hitting exactly 10,000 is tiny. Boundary values have to be chosen on purpose.

questions.q: A team wrote every test as an E2E (browser) test. The suite takes 45 minutes and often breaks for no reason. Which decisions are right?
questions.hint: Think of the pyramid.

options.text: Move calculation cases like boundary values into unit tests
options.why: Unit tests run in milliseconds, and hundreds of cases are cheap to check.

options.text: Keep E2E to just 2-3 main journeys
options.why: With fewer slow, brittle tests, the suite becomes fast and reliable.

options.text: Add even more E2E tests, since they are the most realistic
options.why: They are realistic, but slow and brittle. Adding more makes the problem worse.

options.text: Switch off the tests that break
options.why: Switching tests off throws the protection away. Moving them to the right layer is the fix.

questions.q: Brian's app calls an outside exchange-rate API. The API silently renames `rate` to `exchange_rate`. All of Brian's unit tests are green. Which test would have caught it?
questions.hint: The test that checks the real API's response.

options.text: A contract test: compare the real sandbox response with the schema
options.why: The schema says `rate`, the real response says `exchange_rate`: no match, so the test fails.

options.text: Writing more unit tests
options.why: In a unit test the mock returns the old response we wrote, and never sees the new change.

options.text: A load test
options.why: A load test looks at slowness and failures under a crowd, not at the shape of the response.

options.text: Raising code coverage
options.why: Even if the code lines run, nobody verifies that the response fields are right.

questions.q: Which of these mistakes can only an integration test on real PostgreSQL catch?
questions.hint: Behavior that belongs to the database itself, not to a mock or SQLite.

options.text: Whether the unique index on LOWER(email) blocks duplicates in different letter case
options.why: Index behavior belongs to the database itself. On SQLite or a mock it is different or missing.

options.text: Whether SELECT ... FOR UPDATE locks the row
options.why: Locking is a PostgreSQL feature. With a mock there is no way to verify it.

options.text: Whether the `discountFor()` method calculates 10% correctly
options.why: A pure calculation needs no database. A unit test is enough, and faster.

options.text: Whether a class getter returns the right value
options.why: There is nothing about the database here.

questions.q: Tina ran her k6 script with 100 virtual users and the site fell over, but the script has no sleep. What is the most accurate thing to say about the result?
questions.hint: Do real users fire requests with no pause?

options.text: The result is misleading: non-stop requests put far more pressure on the system than real behavior, so the "100 users" figure isn't realistic
options.why: Real users read a page, think, then click. With a 20ms response, a virtual user without sleep sends about 50 requests a second instead of about 1, so 100 of them push like thousands of real users.

options.text: The result is accurate, because more pressure means safer
options.why: A wrong number gives a wrong estimate of capacity, and you may add or cut servers for no reason.

options.text: Sleep only slows the script down, so it makes no difference
options.why: It makes a huge difference: how many requests per second go out depends directly on sleep.

options.text: It should have been run directly on production, not staging
options.why: Pushing an untested crowd into production is dangerous. The problem is the design of the staging test.

questions.q: What is the purpose of this test, and what makes it fail?
questions.hint: What kind of failures are the two mock responses?

options.text: To check that the provider returns null without crashing on both kinds of failure (503 and timeout); it fails if an exception escapes
options.why: This is a failure-injection test: it verifies that the code handles failures gracefully.

options.text: To check that the courier API returns the correct rates
options.why: There is no successful response here, only two kinds of failure.

options.text: To measure how slow the courier API gets under a crowd
options.why: There is no crowd and no measuring here, just two failed responses.

options.text: The code is only for 503, and the timeout is irrelevant to the test
options.why: The second mock simulates the timeout, and the two go through different exception paths.

questions.q: The nightly contract run fails with "The property charge_cents is required", and the courier now sends `charge`. What is the right next move?
questions.hint: The contract should describe the API as it is now, and the code should follow the contract.

options.text: Remove `required` from the schema so the run goes green again
options.why: Then a missing field passes silently again, and the `?? 0` fallback brings back zero charges.

options.text: Change the schema and example to `charge`, watch the unit test fail, then fix the provider to read `charge`
options.why: The contract now matches the real API, the failing unit test points at the code to change, and both go green together.

options.text: Change only the provider and leave the schema alone
options.why: The schema still describes the old API, so the nightly run keeps failing, and the mock built from the old example hides the change.

questions.q: The courier returns a 503 and checkout shows an error page. What is wrong, and what is the fix?
questions.hint: What does toArray() do with a 5xx answer?

options.text: toArray() throws on a 503 and nothing catches it; wrap the call in try/catch for ExceptionInterface, log, return null
options.why: ExceptionInterface covers 5xx answers, timeouts and bad JSON, so one catch keeps checkout alive.

options.text: Nothing is wrong: HttpClient retries a 503 by itself until it works
options.why: Plain HttpClient does not retry; only RetryableHttpClient does, and even then it gives up eventually.

options.text: Catch only TransportExceptionInterface, which covers all failures
options.why: It covers timeouts and dropped connections, but a 503 arrives as a ServerException and would still escape.

options.text: Add `?? 0` after `$data['charge_cents']`
options.why: The exception is thrown earlier, at toArray(), so this line is never reached. And a silent zero is the original bug.

questions.q: A team is about to run its first chaos test. Which steps are right?
questions.hint: Balance risk against the chance to learn.

options.text: Start with unit tests and staging, breaking one dependency at a time
options.why: A small start carries little risk, and with one change at a time the cause of a result is easy to see.

options.text: Measure the steady state and write down a hypothesis before the experiment
options.why: Without measuring, you can't tell whether anything really changed, and without a hypothesis you learn nothing even when you find a flaw.

options.text: On day one, shut down several services at once in production
options.why: Break many things at once and you can't tell the cause, and the risk is huge.

options.text: Start without deciding when to stop; you will see when the time comes
options.why: Decide before you start what you would have to see to stop. Deciding in the middle of an incident is hard.

questions.q: Steve's test launches two Processes with usleep(50_000) between them. The test is green even on buggy code. What is the most likely cause?
questions.hint: What happens if the first one finishes before the second starts?

options.text: The first process finishes before the second starts, so no race happens
options.why: The sleep is a guess. On a fast machine the whole job finishes within 50ms, and the order becomes one after the other.

options.text: There really is no bug in the code
options.why: The test never causes a race, so it can't tell you whether the bug exists.

options.text: Using Process is the mistake
options.why: Separate processes are the right way. The mistake is how the start times are lined up.

options.text: PHPUnit doesn't support race tests
options.why: PHPUnit just runs tests; causing the race is your test's job, and it can be done with Process.

questions.q: Which of these are part of a good concurrency test?
questions.hint: Truly parallel events, and a check of the final state.

options.text: Giving everyone the same start time (a barrier)
options.why: The processes boot at different times. Without a barrier they don't run off together.

options.text: Checking the stock and the number of orders at the end
options.why: Whatever the buggy order of events, the final state (stock >= 0, sales <= items) catches it.

options.text: Waiting for each process to finish before launching the next
options.why: Then buyers come one after another, and the race never happens.

options.text: Using SQLite because it is fast
options.why: SQLite's locking and isolation behave differently, so it won't reproduce the production race.

questions.q: A client sends the same payment twice with the same Idempotency-Key. What is the correct behavior?
questions.hint: Press the elevator button five times: how many elevators come?

options.text: The second time, return the earlier response and don't charge again
options.why: That is idempotency: no matter how many times the same request arrives, the effect happens once and the response is the same.

options.text: Charge twice, because two requests arrived
options.why: That charges the customer twice, which is exactly what the key exists to prevent.

options.text: Always return an error the second time
options.why: The client lost the response and wants it back. An error leaves it stuck.

options.text: Generate a new key and charge again
options.why: If the server makes up a new key itself, duplicate protection is gone.

questions.q: The migration test below has one important gap. Which one?
questions.hint: When is the old data being loaded?

options.text: The data is loaded after the migration, so how the migration treats old data is never tested
options.why: The risk is that old data breaks the migration. So you load data at the earlier version first, then migrate.

options.text: Using fetchOne is wrong
options.why: fetchOne is fine for reading one value. The problem is when the data is loaded.

options.text: The phone number isn't realistic
options.why: The number is fine. The gap is in the order of the test.

options.text: Running a migration test on a separate database is wrong
options.why: It should run on a separate test database, never on production.

questions.q: Ten buyers hit this code for the last item and stock ends at -3. Why?
questions.hint: What can happen between the SELECT and the UPDATE?

options.text: Several buyers pass the `< 1` check before any of them decrements, because the check and the write are separate steps
options.why: All of them read stock = 1. The fix is one UPDATE with `AND stock > 0` and a check of the affected row count.

options.text: The UPDATE should say `SET stock = :stock` instead of `stock - 1`
options.why: Writing back the value each buyer read would end at 0, but still sell the item to all of them.

options.text: OutOfStock is never thrown
options.why: It is thrown when a buyer reads 0 or less, but by then the damage is done: the early buyers all passed.

options.text: Ten processes are too many for one product
options.why: Real traffic is bigger than that. The code must be correct under any number of buyers.

questions.q: This migration test fails on the user with no phone. Which line is the problem?
questions.hint: What does a user with no phone get as mobile?

options.text: The first line: a new column must never allow NULL
options.why: A nullable column is the safe first step. It lets old rows and old code carry on.

options.text: The second line: UPDATE should not copy existing values
options.why: Copying is fine. The trouble is what happens to rows that have nothing to copy.

options.text: The third line: SET NOT NULL fails on the NULL row, and would also break old servers' INSERTs without mobile
options.why: Make the column NOT NULL only in a later contract migration, after every server writes it.

questions.q: A team has written a race test. Which changes would make it more reliable?
questions.hint: Can the test itself catch the bug? How would you confirm it?

options.text: Running 20 rounds, cleaning the data each time
options.why: A race doesn't always happen. Running many times raises the chance of catching it.

options.text: Running the test against the old buggy code and watching it fail
options.why: You can't know whether a test that has never failed catches anything. Failing on buggy code proves it works.

options.text: Increasing the usleep so the second process starts even later
options.why: Starting later makes the race even less likely.

options.text: Merging as soon as the test is green once
options.why: One green run proves nothing, because a race doesn't always happen.
